messages:
From: Elena Morales <elena.morales@azimuth.ai>
To: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>, procurement@azimuth.ai
Date: 2026-12-05 08:13 PST
Subject: Throughput and reservation questions for Dedicated pool

Hi Markus,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — Azimuth’s platform team was impressed with the latency profile. Before procurement signs the reserved GPU order, our engineering leadership has two items they want clarified so we can finalize the SOW:

1) Your SLA spreadsheet calls out a per-pool steady-state throughput (tokens/sec) and a "queueing behavior" note. Can you confirm how you measure the steady-state number and whether queued requests during brief congestion windows are counted against the committed throughput?

2) If we purchase a 24/7 reserved pool with a small burst buffer, what is the documented process (and timeline) for applying short-term headroom? We need this for our incident runbooks.

I've attached a draft PO+SLA (contract_draft_v2.pdf) and the internal SLA matrix (sla_matrix.xlsx) with redlined columns. Happy to hop on a call if easier.

Best,
Elena
Procurement Lead — Azimuth AI
From: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>
To: Elena Morales <elena.morales@azimuth.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-12-05 09:25 PST
Subject: Re: Throughput and reservation questions for Dedicated pool

Hi Elena — thanks for the clear note and the redlines. Short answers up front:

1) Steady-state throughput: we calculate committed throughput as the 95th-percentile sustained token output over a rolling 24-hour window for the reserved pool, normalized by model family and typical sequence length. Queued requests are NOT charged against the committed throughput metric; they are evaluated separately under our "queueing SLAs" (see attached sla_matrix.xlsx, column F).

2) Short-term headroom: for customers on a reserved contract we offer an on-call playbook to request temporary headroom. Typical response window is 1 business hour for small bursts (<=20% additional capacity for up to 2 hours) and 4 business hours for larger requests, depending on availability. If capacity cannot be granted immediately, we automatically trigger fallback routing to compatible model variants in other regions (with documented latency delta).

I'll let Ben add pricing/crediting details and Jasmine confirm the operational steps we will list in the SOW. If helpful, I can schedule a 30-minute runbook walkthrough later this week.

—Markus
Director, Enterprise Sales Operations
Redwood Inference
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Throughput and reservation questions for Dedicated pool

Elena — quick follow-up on the economics side:

• For brief headroom granted under the on-call playbook we either bill retrospectively at a discounted burst rate or, for large customers who prefer predictability, we convert the usage into a one-time credit applied to the following invoice.
• Queueing: when we detect requests entering the reserved-pool queue beyond the agreed latency tail, we start credit accruals after a 5-minute observation window. Credits are proportional to the duration and affected token volume.

If you want specific credit examples mapped to the numbers in your sla_matrix.xlsx redlines, tell me which rows you care about and I’ll mock up a projection.

Ben
Enterprise Accounts — Redwood Inference
